1.45 The Committee agree with FSSAI that some stringent measures are essential for 
ensuring that the FBOs comply with the FSS Act.  The Committee believes that life time 
licenses are not at all feasible and desirable as the information regarding the food business has 
to be timely updated and checked.  Life time licenses can result in lax compliance with the 
food safety standards whereas requirement of annual returns and renewal of licenses ensures 
checks and balances for compliance with the food safety norms.  
(Para 3.34) 
Action Taken 
1.46 The views of the Committee have been agreed to. FSSAI has examined the feasibility 
of granting license/registration on permanent basis. Apart from its revenue implications, there 
are a few other difficulties in granting permane nt license. At the time of renewal of license, 
presently the food businesses are required to provide details of the technically qualified 
person in charge of operations as well as the person responsible for complying with 
conditions of license.  In case renewal is done away with, the details of these person’s integral 
to food safety would not be captured.  Moreover, at the time of renewal, the licensing 
authority can verify the food safety history of the food business based on which he can renew 

10 
 
the license or decide otherwise.  In the absence of a renewal mechanism, enforcement would 
have to be implemented by means of suspension and cancellation of license. Renewal of 
license/registration acts as a monitoring mechanism.  As a compliance of the FSS Act, Rule s 
and Regulations made thereunder, an FBO has to provide certain details like water testing 
reports, medical examination reports of food handlers and filing of annual returns etc. at the 
time of renewal.  The apprehension is that once licenses are made per manent, the FBO would 
not have much motivation to file these returns as FBO would stand disconnected from 
FSSAI/Regulator after the issue of permanent license. Enforcement again would then perforce 
be done through suspension and cancellation of license. Th erefore, there is no proposal to 
issue life time licenses.   
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.47 The Committee also notes that the rejection rate of the licenses for renewal is very 
low in the country.  The Committee recommends that licenses for FBOs should n ot be issued 
blindly and a well established mechanism should be developed for scrutinizing such FBOs 
who apply for renewal of the license.  In developed countries like US, application of renewal 
licenses is taken seriously and there is a high rate of rejections due to non-conforming of food 
standards.  FSSAI should also examine the FBO’s previous track record with regards to 
compliance with the FSS Act.  Any previous non -compliance should be taken seriously.  The 
Committee recommends expediting the developm ent of an e -portal that will create a

1.86 The Committee is not convinced with the sampling procedure, analysis time and

Action Taken 
1.87 FSSAI has conducted a survey on quality of milk. It initiated a Nationwide 
Qualitative Screening of milk samples for on -spot qualitative and quantitative analysis of 
milk. The survey was  initiated in May, 2018 with a sample size   of   6432 samples taken 
from 1100 towns with a population of over 50,000 across all 29 States and 7 Union 
Territories for qualitative and quantitative analysis. Scope of NMSQS 2018 covered 3 quality 
parameters ( Fat, SNF and water), 13 common adulterants (vegetable oil/fat, 
detergents/caustic soda, hydrogen peroxide, sugar, glucose, urea, starch, Maltodextrin, boric 
acid, ammonium sulphate, nitrates, cellulose, and neutralizer; and 3 contaminants (antibiotics, 
pesticides, aflatoxin M1,).  All the 6432 samples were collected and analysed qualitatively 
immediately onsite in mobile vans and nearly 30% of those samples that tested positive for 
any of the adulterants and/or contaminants were tested quantitatively in lab oratory to 
ascertain whether the samples were compliant or non-compliant to limits set.    
1.88 As per NMSQS final report released in October, 2019 -   
- About 7%  samples were found to be unsafe for consumption due to presence of 
harmful contaminants in e xcess of specified limits coming mainly from poor quality 
of feed, irresponsible use of antibiotics and poor farm practices 
- Only 12 out of total 6432 samples had adulterants that affect the quality of milk 
- About 41% of milk samples of the total were, h owever, non -compliant with 
reference to one or the other quality parameters [fat, Solid not -fat (SNF), sugar and 
maltodextrin] but were without any safety issues.   
1.89 Details of survey are  available at https://www.fssai.gov.in/home .   Thus, the survey  
results indicate clearly that milk being sold in India is largely safe for consumption.  This is 
contrary to the popular perception carried by the consumers owing to misrepresented 
information for various reasons including deceitful campaigns and unsubstantiated reports

1.104 Under sub-regulation 2.3.5 of Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restriction 
on Sales) Regulations, 20 11, use of acetylene gas, commonly known as carbide gas, in 
artificial ripening of fruits has been prohibited.  As an alternative, ripening of fruits by using 
ethylene gas at a concentration upto 100 ppm (100µ/L) depending upon the crop, variety and 
maturity is now permitted.  Ethylene is a safer alternative. it may be mentioned that ethylene 
is a hormone which is produced in the fruits naturally to facilitate their ripening   in a natural 
way.   
1.105 As also suggested by the Standing Committee, periodic advisories have been issued to 
the State Food Authorities to monitor use of calcium carbide   for artificial ripening of fruits 
and take stringent action for violation of the provisions. Further, whenev er a specific instance 
is reported about use of banned carbide gas for ripening, the matter is immediately taken up 
with Food Safety Commissioners of States/UTs for taking strict action in respect of reported 
instances.  
1.106 Further, a Guidance Note on a rtificial ripening of fruits has been published to create 
awareness among food business operators/ traders, consumers and other stakeholders related 
to various aspects of artificial ripening of fruits. It also includes Standard Operating 
Procedure detailing all facets of artificial ripening using ethylene gas and its reliable sources. 
In addition, a direction was issued on 16.08.2018 on use of ‘ethephon’ in powder form for 
artificial ripening of fruits and the same was uploaded on FSSAI’s website for wider 
publicity. It clarifies that ethephon in powder form may also be used as a source of ethylene 
gas provided that it shall be packed in sachets and shall not come in direct contact with fruits.

should be replicated in all the States and Union Territories. This will help in preventing the 
use of industrial ice in place of edible ice and ensure that  industrial/contaminated ice is not 
used in drinks. State Regulatory Authorities should conduct regular inspections at ice 
manufacturing sites and strict actions must be taken against manufacturing units and vendors 
who manufacture/use ice from contaminate d water. Timely inspections have to be conducted 

21 
 
at the premises. The ice that is manufactured for preservation and the ice for edible purposes 
should not be manufactured at the same location.  
(Para 5.39) 
Action Taken 
1.109 With a view to check misuse of non-edible ice as edible ice, a decision has been 
taken and conveyed   to all States/UTs that food colour (Indigo Carmine or Brilliant blue up 
to 10 ppm) must be used in production of non -edible ice, including non -edible ice blocks 
coming in contact with food products during preservation/storage/transportation of perishable 
food commodities, to give it a bluish look/appearance so as to enable clear differentiation 
with edible ice which must remain colourless. All Food Business Operators engaged in 
production /use of edible/non -edible ice have been instructed to ensure visible distinction 
between edible and non-edible ice by using food colour as mentioned above in non -edible ice 
w.e.f. 1st June, 2018. Food Safety Commissioners of States/UTs have been asked to  enhance 
surveillance/enforcement on sale of non -edible ice so as to ensure compliance of this 
directive.  
 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.110   The Committee desires the FSSAI to ensure that all the provisions laid down in the 
FSS Regulations are being followed by all the importers and imported food products fulfil all 
the required standards and international benchmarks. The Committee recommends that 
FSSAI should frame specific guidelines for the food products that have been banned 
elsewhere in the world. Special care should be taken to ensure that expired food items do not 
get clearance and the country should not be a dumping ground for food item s rejected 
elsewhere due to quality issues.  
(Para 5.54) 
Action Taken 
 
1.111 To streamline the food import system, FSSAI has an online system known as F ood 
Import Clearance System (FICS). The FICS is integrated with the customs’ ICE -GATE 
(Indian Customs Electronic Commerce/Electronic Data interchange (EC/EDI) Gateway) 
system. 
 
1.112 Risk Management System (RMS) is implemented in ICE -GATE wherein, based on 
the risk categorization of the food, compliance history of the importer and country of origin 
etc. co nsignments are referred to FSSAI for clearance. Such food articles  are subjected to 
scrutiny of documents, visual inspection, sampling and testing in order to determine their 
conformance to the safety and quality standards laid down under various Food Safe ty and 
Standards Regulations. If sample is found conforming a No Objection Certificate (NOC) is 
generated and in case of otherwise, Non -Conforming Report (NCR) is generated.  For food 
consignments imported into India, a special condition has been introduce d through an 
amendment in Regulation 2 (b) (6) of Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017 
whereby food products having a valid shelf life of not less than sixty per cent or three months 
before expiry at the time of import, whichever is less, s hall not be cleared by Customs. As a 
result, entry of food products nearing expiry or after expiry date is prohibited. Food Import 
samples are tested with reference to the Standards prescribed under various FSS Regulations. 
The Standards notified by FSSAI are globally benchmarked while being consistent with 
Indian context. It is unlikely that a food product which is banned outside is allowed to enter 

22 
 
into the country as the Indian Standards are harmonized with Codex and other International 
Standards.    
 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.113 The Committee also recommends close monitoring of imported food items once the 
food item enters the market. Any quality issue that is reported across the country should be 
taken seriously. In the eventuality of ban on imported item entering the Indian mark et, the 
information should be immediately shared with the industry as well as the consumers. There 
should be a recall plan for immediate withdrawal of imported food items.   Based on the 
advisory issued by FSSAI on 11.06.2018, Director General of Foreign T rade (DGFT), 
prohibited the import of milk and milk products (including chocolates and chocolate products 
and candies/confectionary/food preparations with milk or milk solids as an ingredient) from 
China till 23.12.2018. 
(Para 5.55) 
Action Taken  
1.114 The Licensing Authority cancels or suspends food import license if there is 
contravention of the provisions of FSS(Import) Regulations or the Food Safety and Standards 
(Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.  
1.115 Data regarding rejections of imported food consignments are also being uploaded on 
monthly basis on FSSAI website. A monthly report on rejections are also sent to the 
Embassies of the respective Countries along with the reasons for rejections and necessary  
applicable FSS Rules and Regulations.  Further, Food Import Rejection Alert system has 
been developed to capture non-compliances of all imported food products. 
1.116 Information in respect of recall plan has been furnished in reply to Para 3.23 above.  
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.117  The Committee has been given to understand that presently it takes five to eight days 
to get import clearance for a   food consignment while there has been demand to reduce this 
time for ease of doing business. The Committee recommends that steps should be  taken to 
reduce the import clearance time but not at the cost of quality and safety aspects. Especially 
with respect to the perishable items. FSSAI should aim on reducing the import clearance time 
significantly so that only fresh food items reach the consumers.  
(Para 5.56) 
Action Taken 
1.118 FSSAI has taken many steps for reducing the clearance time of Imported Food items 
such as: 
a) Introduction of provisional No Objection Certificate (PNOC) for imported pre -
packaged retail food articles vide directions dated 01.05.2018, in addition to Provisional 
No Objection Certificates (PNOC) for imported food items having short shelf -life (less 
than 7 days) such as fresh fruits & vegetables which require special storage conditions.  
With the PNOC, an importer can move t he imported food consignment to a   well -
equipped storage facility till receipt of the lab test results, but can’t release the same in 
the market. This step results into reduction of the demurrage charges. 
 

23 
 
b) FSSAI has identified laboratories in exporting countries viz. Bangladesh and Bhutan for 
prior testing of food samples.The test analysis certificate issued by these laboratories 
are accepted at Indian points of entry for food import clearance and such consignments 
are not subject to further testing upon arrival in India. 
 
   c)   A regular monitoring of time taken for testing of imported food items by labs is being 
carried out regularly. The poor performing labs are removed from the system. 
 
1.119 As a result of the above measures, time taken in import clearance has been reduced 
significantly.

Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 The Committee notes that FSSAI is the apex regulatory body for food safety in the 
country and the Preamble to FSS Act inter -alia seeks to lay down science based standards for 
articles of food and ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human con sumption.  
Food Safety is thus a specialized job and FSSAI being a science based organization should be 
equipped with proper tools and capabilities and headed by someone with the requisite 
technical acumen and appropriate expertise to address the challengi ng task of food regulation 
for a country like India.  Engaging man-power with technical skill and competence, therefore, 
becomes imperative for effective rendering of important mandate given to FSSAI.  The 
Committee is of the opinion that the regulatory body should be run by experts/scientists in the 
food sector with bureaucratic support.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
qualifications   and procedures of selection and appointment of Chairman and CEO of FSSAI 
be reviewed so that the best profe ssional with domain expertise are selected for this onerous 
regulatory responsibility. While reviewing and modifying the process of selection and 
appointment of Chairman and CEO, the Government may take a cue from similar regulatory 
mechanisms functioning in some of the developed countries like USA, UK, Australia etc.  
 
(Para 1.22) 
   
Action Taken  
 
2.2 The process of selection of Chairperson, FSSAI who is the head of this organization, 
has been laid down in section 5 & 6 of the Food Safety and Standards Ac t, 2006. In terms of 
Section 5 (3) of the Act, the Central Government appoints Chairperson, FSSAI from amongst 
the persons of eminence in the field of food science or from amongst the persons from 
administration who have been/are associated with the subjec t in the level not below the rank 
of Secretary to the Government of India. Chairperson and CEO are appointed on the basis of 
administrative experience in diverse fields . They work with aid and advice of technical 
experts available in Scientific Panels of F SSAI on different subjects. Experience, so far, has 
shown that they have functioned very effectively in discharge of their responsibilities.  
 
Recommendation /Observation 
   
2.3 The Committee recommends that proper guidelines for selection of members in the

have some members with industrial experience so that the diverse views from other se ctors 
are also accommodated.

2.12 The Committee underlines the need for an effective allocation of financial resources

2.14 The implementation and enforcement of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 rests 
primarily with the State/UT Governments, for which regular surveillance, monitoring and  
inspection are required to be undertaken by them.  The Committee however notes that many 
States do not have a separate food safety Department.  The Committee is of the view that 
food adulteration, lack of quality checks, misleading labelling, sale of defective food products 
etc. that have become the norm these days are primarily an offshoot of absence of a dedicated 
and robust food safety apparatus at the State Level. The Joint Committee of Parliament on the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration (Amendment), 197 4 had recommended long back that for 
effective implementation of the Act, a separate food safety department under the control of 
the Director of Health should be established in all the States.  Endorsing the same view, the 
Committee strongly recommends est ablishment of a separate agency or Department of Food 
Safety in each State for enforcing a robust food safety mechanism in the country.  The 
Committee also recommends that the creation of a dedicated food regulatory mechanism in 
each State be taken up by t he Union Government with the State Governments at the highest 
level.    
 

28 
 
2.15 The Committee notes that there is no uniformity in the food safety infrastructure 
across the country.  Some States do not even have a food safety department and a food safety 
appellate tribunal.  The food testing laboratories lack functional equipments as well as 
technical manpower.  This inadequate arrangement has failed to control food adulteration in 
the country.   Therefore, the Committee recommends removal of this existing in consistency 
and introduction of a uniform structure across the country.  The Central Government should 
work in cooperation with the State Government to establish a uniform food safety regulatory 
regime in the country.  It is also very important for the foo d testing laboratories across 
States/UTs to follow uniform procedure/methodology and guidelines so that consistent results 
are obtained.   
(Para 2.17 & 2.20) 
Action Taken  
 
i. The issue of setting up separate food safety department has been taken up with 
States/UTs regularly. As per the data shared by States/UTs in Quarterly Progress 
Report on State Specific recommendations of CAG and the PSC, process of creation 
of separate food safety department has been initiated in 6 States/UTsviz Andhra 
Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Goa &Uttrakhand. 
ii. FSSAI had initially proposed in the draft amendments the setting up of the ‘State 
Food Authority’ to be headed by the Chief Secretary of the State for coordination and 
supervision for enforcement of the Act. However, some of the State Governments did 
not find favour with such a proposal considering it as transgression of their legislative 
powers in the federal structure. It was also felt that the structure of food safety 
departments of States/ UTs cannot be uniform but would necessarily vary considering 
peculiar facts in State/ UT such as demography, geography, terrain, spread & reach of 
food businesses, food habits of general populace. Therefore, on reconsideration, the 
proposal to have an independent Food Safety Department and State Food Authority in 
each State/ UT has been dropped and is not among the amendment proposals 
submitted by FSSAI to the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
2.16 In some States/UTs officers in Health Department are holding additional charge of 
food safety department.  Section 30 of the FSS Act states that the State Government shall 
appoint the Commissioner of Food Safety for the State for efficient implementation of food 
safety and standards and other requirements la id down under the Act.  The Section spells out 
the functions of the Commissioner of Food Safety in terms of  (i) regulating manufacture, 
storage, distribution or sale of any article of food in the interest of public health, (ii) carrying 
out survey of the industrial units engaged in manufacture or processing of food, (iii) 
conducting or organising training programmes for the personnel, (iv) generating awareness of 
food safety, (v) ensuring an efficient and uniform implementation of the standards and (vi) 
sanctioning prosecution for offences etc. The Committee understands that the Food Safety 
Commissioner has to perform a wide range of functions.  It, therefore, recommends that the 
officer should be conversant with food science and technology and should be a whole time 
officer.  Part time arrangement for such important functions in many States/UTs will not 
serve the interest of the Act. 
(Para 2.18)

‘’rich in..., contains added....., fortified with...., added with...., natural, herbal, organic’’ etc.

2.33 The Committee takes note of the fact that the proprietary food has been defined in

the testing need efficiently. This will distribute the workload and evenly manage the samples

food testing labs so that there is no delay in sending the samples to the labs and results are

20 districts of the State. However, given the large size of our co untry and huge population,

common man.

Action Taken 
 
3.111 Along the lines of the recommendations of the Standing Committee, FSSAI has 
scheme to provide 50 mobile food testing laboratories, called as Food Safety on Wheels 
(FSWs) to the States/UTs based on their readiness especially in terms of av ailability of 
manpower with them for running of FSWs. These FSWs would not only address the issue of 
lack of food testing infrastructure in the remote areas but also cater to the basic analytical 
needs of consumers. Apart from testing and training, the FSW s also help the regulatory staff 
or the field functionaries in the States/UTs to enhance their outreach; and, also help in 
conducting surveillance activities even in far-flung areas. 
 
3.112 FSWs are utilized for (i) surveillance and creating awareness rega rding the food 
safety in remote areas in the State, large public congregations, schools and consumer 
organisations; (ii) transporting samples picked from remote areas to the nearest food testing 
laboratory; (iii) education of the consumers in various aspec ts of food safety laws and 
common hygiene practices; (iv) on the spot test facilities for qualitative adulteration of 
common food items like ghee, milk, khoya, sweets, edible oil, non -permitted food colours in 
various foods like namkeens, spices, prepared foods etc.  
 
3.113 Each FSW can test >54 parameters qualitatively across seven different food 
categories. In addition, each FSW has a provision for performing simple microbiological 
tests if the States so desire. The FSW is provided at a cost of ~ 50 lakh INR each, including a 
recurring grant of Rs. 5 Lakhs per year for 3 years towards Petrol, Oil, Lubricants & 
consumables. As on date, 40 FSWs have been sanctioned/delivered to 29 States/UTs. Since 
there are fund constraints in FSSAI, States/UTs may also hav e their own FSWs. Some of the 
States like J&K and Union Territory of Chandigarh have their own mobile testing labs also.

3.124  The Committee observes that loose edible oils are prone to adulteration and even if 
edible oil sellers comply with food safety regulations and standards at the first point of sale, 
there is no guarantee that the oil would remain unadulterated as they pass through several 
hands. There have been countless instances of sale of adulterated loose oils which have 
resulted in masses being afflicted by dropsy. The Committee gathers that Delhi –based  
consumer organisation, namely, Consumer Voice, had in the year 201 6 collected samples of 
loose edible oils of eight varieties, namely Mustard, Sesame, Groundnut and Cottonseed from 
15 States and got them tested on safety as well as quality parameters in a NABL accredited 
laboratory. The laboratory results revealed that a dulteration was found in loose oil samples 
collected from all 15 States and 8% samples of coconut oil, 74.07% samples of cottonseed 
oil, 74% samples of mustard oil were found adulterated. Adulterated edible oil is one of the 
main reasons behind several dis eases like cardiac arrest, cancer, epidemic dropsy, liver 
damage, paralysis etc. Without packaging, batch number or FSSAI license number it is very 
difficult to trace the source of the problem. in the event of health epidemic breaking out due 
to adulterated edible oils.   
 
3.125 With a view to safeguard the interests of consumers, the Committee would like to 
recommend to the Central Govt to impress upon the State Governments to ensure that edible 
oils are retailed in packaged form only.  
 
3.126 The Committee simultaneously observes that there is another dimension to the sale 
of edible oil in loose form which should not be lost sight of. Small consumers especially daily 
wage labourers and the rural poor purchase loose edible oils out of their payment on daily  
basis. They cannot afford to buy oil sold in pack of one litre or more and therefore buy loose 
edible oil in small quantity. It is, therefore, absolutely essential for the FSSAI to push for 
smaller packages of 100ml and 200 ml of edible oil.  
(Para 5.19, 5.20 & 5.21)

3.135  The Committee observes that in India the GM food imports require approvals under 
the Environment Protection Act of 1986 and the Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006. 
While the former law covers the environmental impacts of the food products, the latter 
assesses the food’s impact on human health. Since no regulation has been finalized for GM 
products, it is still banned in the country. Further, even after the Environment Ministry gives 
clearances for imports, permission is also required under the food safe ty law but importers 
have got away without having the mandatory approval under the Food Safety and Standards 
Act. A large number of products are coming in India with GM ingredients but neither 
consumers nor authorities are aware of what is inside because t here is nothing mentioned on 
the label. Taking the above fact into account, the Committee recommends formulation of 
regulations to the effect that those importing foods must provide mandatory declaration on 
the label mentioning that ‘this food is from GM f ree source’. Countries like China, Australia 
and the European Union nations have strict regulations about GM foods labelling so that the 
consumer makes informed choices.   
3.136 The Committee observes that even after more than a decade of enactment of FSS Act, 
a regulatory vacuum exists in the import of GM Food. FSSAI has neither put the regulations 
for such approvals in place nor taken any measures to stop the imports. The Committee 
recommends that the FSSAI should urgently finalise “Guidelines for safety assessment of 
food derived by GM technology” and implement them within three months of presentation of 
the Report to the Parliament. FSSAI should also work to upgrade the GM food testing 
infrastructure and make use of the already present laboratories in th e country and equip them 
with latest technology.   
3.137 The Committee is perturbed to note that the action (or lack of it) in regulation of GM 
foods by FSSAI has been painstakingly slow. Recently FSSAI had decided to have the 
labelling norms for genetically modified food products in order to give informed choice to the 

70 
 
consumers. All food products having total Genetically Engineered (GE) ingredients 5% or 
more shall be labelled. The labelling shall be –“Contains GMO/Ingredients derived from 
GMO’. The absen ce of regulation for a decade in respect of GM foods would have caused 
irreversible damage to the consumers, who are the core constituency for whom FSSAI was 
set up. The Committee strongly censures the FSSAI for this lackadaisical attitude and 
implores upon it to pull up its socks and ensure that the regulation made in respect to GM 
foods be implemented within a time bound period and also provide training to its personnel 
involved in regulation of GM foods. The Committee also directs that FSSAI should also 
educate the citizens of the country as to what constitutes GM foods as a vast majority of 
people are not aware of the concept of GM foods.  
(Para 5.50, 5.51 & 5.52)

3.146 To ensure consumer’s trust, there is need of genuineness and authenticity of foods 
claimed as ‘Organic’. To ensure this, a regulatory mechanism backed by a robust certification 
system is required. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has the mandate to 
regulate manufacture, distribute, sale or import  “organic foods” as per the provisions laid 
under Section 22 of the Food Safety Standards Act, 2006. Organic foods are regulated by 
Food Safety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017 notified under the provisions 
of the Act. Food Safety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017 stipulate  that - 
 the organic food offered or promoted for sale shall comply with the provisions of one 
of the systems namely Participatory Guarantee System for India (PGS -India) 
implemented by Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare or the National 
Programme for Organic Production (NPOP) implemented by APEDA under Ministry

addition to the Food Safety and Standard Authority of India’s organic logo (Jaivik 
Bharat logo).  The consumers can easily identify the organic foods by looking at the 
Jaivik Bharat logo and can get assured about these being genuinely organic. 
 To address the difficulties of the small and marginal farmers/ small FBOs, Organic 
food which is marketed through direct sales to the end consumer by the small original 
producer or producer organisation is exempted from provision of the certification 
system i.e., NPOP or PGS -India. Small original producer or producer organisation is 
the one whose annual turnover is not exceeding Rs 12 Lakhs per annum.

Working Group (WG) was constituted by the Scientific Committee under the Scientific Panel

(i) To collect and collate relevant scientific data, either from the industry or available in

(ii) The evaluation of the data and risk assessment of the food colors for their use in

 It was suggested that for using combination of colours, the maximum limit for

3.  After completion of the task by the WG, the final report will be placed before the

4. The aforesaid task is of scientific nature which requires collection and collation of 
relevant data and their detailed examination in view of various aspects of human risks. It is 
therefore, difficult to assign a fixed time frame for completion of the work.  Five meetings of 
the WG have been conducted so far. WG carried out a detailed review of the standards and 
provisions related to food colours.   The WG has almost completed i ts task. The 
recommendations of the WG are as under: 
 
(i) Nomenclature: WG suggested to have no distinction between natural and synthetic 
food colours and decided to call them simply as “food colours”. It was recommended 
that each food colour shall be declared on the label of the product using their INS 
number with full nomenclature as prescribed under regulations. 
(ii) Colouring foods will not fall under the definition of food colours.  
(iii) Maximum limit of food colours in combination : It was decided that no maximum 
limit for colours in combination can be fixed in absence of any scientific basis. 
(iv) Food Colour - Preparation and Mixtures: It was suggested revising the standard to 
generalise for food colours irrespective of its type-natural or synthetic. 
(v) Aluminium Lakes of Colouring Matters :  Provision for lake colours was revised 
based on specification laid down by Joint FAO/WHO Expert committee on Food 
Additives (JECFA).  
(vi) Vertical standards on Food Colours : The specifications for all the fo od colours 
listed in Food Safety and Standards Regulations (FSSR) including those which do not

(vii) Risk assessment of food colours permitted in FSSR 
WG carried out risk assessment of the food colours having lowest Acceptable Daily 
Intakes (ADI), i.e. Canthaxanthi n and Erythrosine. Accordingly, their limits in

a uniform Laboratory Testing System in the country. FSSAI will have to ensure that 
these manuals on Method of Analysis and Good Laboratory Practices are diligently 
followed by all the FTLs in the country. The Committee observes that FSSAI has not 
paid the desired attention to the prevailing inadequate facilities for checking the food 
articles on all parameters in the labs. The pers isting flawed practice of deeming a food 
article safe even when it fails on some parameters raises serious concern about the 
accuracy of the testing methodology. The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to 
guide the Laboratories about the specific food s afety parameters on which any food 
article should be mandatorily checked. Imported food should only be allowed in the 
market when it has passed the mandatory parameters as per the global norms. 
 
(Para 3.85) 
 
 The Committee recommends that FSSAI should expe dite the process of 
amending the FSS Rule, 2011 for incorporating the provision of 14 days time period for 
a referral laboratory to submit their test reports.  The Committee further reiterates its 
recommendation for adoption of best international practices  by the National Referral 
Laboratories with respect to standards for testing and validation.  
(Para 3.89) 
 
NABL ACCREDITATION OF LABS 
 
 The Committee strongly recommends FSSAI to accelerate the drive to accredit 
the remaining FTLs that have not been notified by it so far. The Committee also urges 
the Ministry and FSSAI to take up the matter of accreditation with the States and 
ensure speedy notification of the State Food Testing Laboratories under Section 43(1) of 
FSS Act, 2006. Operation of most of the existing labs without NABL accreditation raises 
serious apprehension over the FTLs quality and technical competence. The Committee 
is worried that most of these labs may not have undergone a third party 
assessment/audit. The Committee also opines that F SSAI should take strict measures 
against the labs that have repeatedly been failing in quality assessment/audit. Labs that 
are already NABL accredited should also be investigated periodically. 

88 
 
 
(Para 3.92) 
STATUS OF MANPOWER IN LABS 
 As per data submitted by FSSAI, there are 452 Public/Food Analysts against the 
estimated requirement of almost 800 food analyst. The Committee concludes that many 
laboratories may be operating without any Food Analysts. This is a sorry state of affair 
and speaks volumes of the inadequate technical competence of the FTLs in the country. 
The Committee would like FSSAI to urgently take up the matter of increasing the 
number of personnel in the laboratory with the States. The Committee underlines an 
urgent need for the States/UTs to  work in close partnership with FSSAI for ensuring a 
better food safety mechanism in the country. The Committee further urges the 
States/UTs to follow the guidance document for setting up a food testing laboratory. 
(Para 3.97) 
 
 The Committee has taken cog nizance of the progress made in regard to 
implementation of the Central Sector Schemes for 'Strengthening of Food Testing 
System' in the country.  It finds that out of a total outlay of Rs. 481.95 crore, a sum of 
Rs. 312.98 crore has been sanctioned/releas ed to States/UTs, while substantial balance 
amount to the tune of Rs. 168.97 crore still remained unspent as some of proposals are 
still under consideration. Non-utilisation of 35% funds and that too for a Central sector 
projects does not augur well and le aves a quantum made on the fixed management of 
the Ministry. 
(Para 3.103) 
 
STRENGTHENING OF STATE FOOD TESTING LABORATORIES (SFTLs) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that out of the total target of upgrading 42 
SFTLS, upgradation of 39 SFTLS spread over 29 States/UTs have been taken up.  The 
Committee desires that upgradation of the remaining 3 labs may also be started at the 
earliest.  
(Para 3.104) 
 
 Notwithstanding the fact that the Committee has been emphasizing on the need 
of recruitment of Food Analysts in the country, there has been no perceptible change in 
the situation. The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to expedite the 
recruitment of Food Analysts in the country and also take up the matter with the State 
Governments. Special attention should also be paid on the qualification of the Food 
Analyst so that only technically qualified and experienced personnel are recruited on 
the post of Food  Analysts. There is also a need to develop a monitoring mechanism for 
the work done by Food Analysts so that they are not tempted into giving false reports.  
 
(Para 3.108) 
FOOD SAFETY ON WHEELS (FSW) 
 
 The Committee notes the potential of mobile food testi ng laboratories, Food 
Safety on Wheels (FSWs) and recommends FSSAI to upgrade and increase the number 
of FSWs especially in remote areas. The Committee reiterates its recommendation on 
utilising the rich demographic dividend of the country and urges FSSAI to conduct 
extensive training program for the youth. The Committee strongly recommends FSSAI 

89 
 
to devise a special training program for the youth for operating these mobile testing 
labs.   
(Para 3.114) 
 
 The Committee feels that awareness on food safety and quality provisions and 
implication of FSS Act and its regulation is still lacking. The Committee understands 
that the massive outreach programme of FSSAI viz. 'Eat Right India' Swasth Bharat 
Yatra etc. would go a  long way in spreading awareness about the provisions of the 
FSSAI and its regulation.  The Committee, therefore, feels that a lot more needs to be 
done by FSSAI on these fronts. 
(Para 3.120) 
REGULATION OF FOOD ITEMS 
 
 The Committee notes the provisions of proposed amendments in Section 59 A in 
the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006 intended to curb the rampant adulteration of 
the food products and the penal provision thereon. The Committee, however, 
recommends the Minis try to expedite the process of the proposed amendments so that 
the growing menace of adulteration of milk and dairy products having serious health 
implication is combated in right earnest.  
(Para 3.123) 
 
REGULATION OF PRESERVATIVES/CHECMICALS USED FOR STOR AGE FOR 
FISHES, ARTIFICIAL RIPENING OF FRUITS/VEGETABLES AND EDIBLE ICE 
 
 Taking note of rampant sale of loose edible oil in village and remote towns, the 
Committee recommends FSSAI to take up the issue with States and UTs Government. 
Keeping in view the need of economically weaker section of the society, edible oil 
companies ha s appropriately been allowed to make edible oil available in small 
pouches/sachets. The Committee, nevertheless, recommends FSSAI to carry out regular 
inspection in FBOs where large scale oil is consumed especially in shops where the 
leftover cooking oil i s being used multiple times. The Committee is of the view that the 
FSSAI should conduct regular training for acquainting the FBOs about the safe 
disposal of the oil and understand how repeated heating of the oil dangerously changes 
the fatty acid composition of the oil.  
(Para 3.130) 
PLASTIC IN FOOD ITEMS/WATER 
 
 The Committee observes that many street food stalls keep selling fried food 
reusing the same oil. The Committee understands that FSSAI has issued regulation on 
limit for TPC to a maximum of 25% beyond which the cooking oil is unsafe for 
consumption.  The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to conduct on the spot 
inspection in food stalls to ensure the permissible 25% limit for Total Polar Compounds 
(TPC) is not crossed and penal action taken a gainst those defaulting FBOs. Moreover, 
the Committee is of the view that mere issuance of advisory is not the solution and 
FSSAI will have to take more pro -active steps to facilitate the mandatory inclusion of 
street food vendors in this initiative. 
(Para 3.134) 
 
 
 

90 
 
REGULATION OF GENETICALLY MODIFIED (GM) FOODS 
 
 The Committee in its 110 th Report had raised concerns over the snail pace of 
drafting of regulations and guidelines with respect to the labelling norms, safety 
assessment of food derived by GM technology etc.  The Committee is disappointed to 
note that even after two years of the p resentation of this Report, the regulations have 
not been notified. The Committee, therefore, strongly urges upon the Ministry to 
expedite the process of notification of Regulation on GM foods so that the import of 
food products is regulated and every food  product with a GM ingredient is inspected. 
The Committee seeks to be informed about the strategy chalked out for making public 
awareness campaign by FSSAI on the concept and constitution of GM Foods and its 
implication.  
(Para 3.140) 
 
REGULATION OF IMPORTED FOOD ITEMS 
 
 The Committee observes that the data submitted by the Ministry is outdated as 
the same pertains to the year 2016 -17. The Committee recommends the Ministry to 
submit latest data regarding clearance of imported food through different points o f 
entry being handled by FSSAI and other points of entry which are being handled by 
customs.   
(Para 3.143) 
REGULATION OF ORGANIC FOOD 
 
 The Committee appreciates that FSSAI understands the difficulties faced by 
small FBOs in accessing the market. The Committee, however, is quite apprehensive of 
the proposal for inclusion of a provision for "aggregator/ intermediary" in the FSS 
(Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017.  The Committee, in this regard, recommends that 
FSSAI should take necessary measures to ensu re that the small FBOs are not exploited 
and get adequate remuneration of their produce. 
 
(Para 3.149) 
REGULATION OF FORTIFIED FOOD 
 
 The Committee recommends that the observation/message, enshrined in the 
report titled “Food Fortification in India: Status and Road Ahead - Need for a Strategic 
Shift for Further Scale Up” detailing State best practices and supply chain models of 
Select states, be implemented by other States. The Committee believes that the children 
benefitted under two cherished programmes of the country viz. Mid -Day Meal (MDM) 
and Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) would be beneficiary of fortified 
foods.  
(Para 3.152) 
 
REGULATION OF FOOD IN EATERIES 
 
 The Committee desires that the proposed amendments in FSS (Packaging &  
Labelling) Regulation with regard to display of information in food service 
establishment be notified without delay. The Committee also recommends that apart 
from display of information relating to calorific value of food and nutritive value of 
food in th e menu, quantity of portion should also be specified in the menu. The 
Committee also reiterates its recommendation for periodic inspection of basic 

91 
 
infrastructure of food service establishment and the adoption of standard hygiene 
practices therein.    
(Para 3.155) 
PACKAGING 
 
 The Committee recommends FSSAI to escalate its efforts in implementing food 
safety norms and guidelines in view of the outbreak of pandemic Covid -19 and 
thereafter in the wake of unlocking Phase. The Committee further recommends FSSAI 
to collaborate with different groups of street vendors and FBOs and increase the reach 
of its digital training program on hygiene issues for ensuing food safety standards 
during this peculiar phase. The Committee opines that the need of the hour is to draw  
area specific programs for street food vendors and strict adherence to safety practices 
such as using disinfectant, wearing protective gears, maintaining social distancing etc. 
in the FBO premises.  
(Para 3.158) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendati on that FSSAI should create a food 
advertising monitoring cell to monitor all the food advertisements and disseminate the 
information regarding misleading advertisements to the public. 
 
(Para 3.166) 
 
 The Committee takes note of a dedicated interaction portal for making food 
purchasers into smart, alert and aware consumers. The Committee would like the 
FSSAI to take certain initiatives for spreading awareness among the rural consumers 
too since these co nsumers may face difficulty in accessing the FSSAI portal and a 
helpline number instead would certainly give voice to their complaints.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends to FSSAI to have dedicated helpline number for addressing the 
complaints of such consumers.  
(Para 3.170) 
INFORMATION EDUCATION COMMUNICATION (IEC) 
 
 The Committee notes the FSSAI's initiative in digitising the different aspects of 
food safety infrastructure and record management to ensure not only better data 
management and easy accessibility but also transparency in food business management.  
Nevertheless, considering the low level of digital literacy in the country, the Committee 
recommends FSSAI to also ensure that the FBOs get the required capacity and training 
to access these platforms. 
(Para 3.174)

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this One Hundred Twenty Second  Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in the One Hundred Twentieth  
Report on Demands for Grants 2020-21 (Demand No. 4) of the Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
2. The One Hundred Twentieth Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of 
Lok Sabha on 6th March, 20 20.  Action Taken Note of the Ministry on the recommendations 
contained in the Report was received from the Ministry on 13th July, 2020.   
 
3. The Committee had noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the 120th Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuant to the direction of Chairman, Rajya Sabha dated  24th 
September, 2004. 
 
4. The Committee made a total of 27 recommendations in its 120 th Report.  Out of the 27 
recommendations, a total number of 8 recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry , has 
been  categorized under Chapter I and there are a total number of 2 recommendations, which the 
Committee does not desire to pursue in view o f the Ministry’s replies,  has been categorized under 
Chapter II.  A total number of 12 recommendations/ observations in respect of which replies of the 
Ministry have not been accepted by the Committee and  the Committee has made further 
recommendations the reon, has been categorized under Chapter III while a total number of 5 
recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been 
received, has been categorized under Chapter IV.   
 
5. The Committee considered the Draft Re port and adopted the same in its meeting held on 
the 7th September, 2020.

REPORT 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the 
Recommendations/ Observations contained in the Committee's One Hundred Twentieth Report on 
Demands for Grants 2020-21 (Demand No. 4) of the Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorized as follows:  
 
(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted b y the Ministry:  2.24, 3.9, 
3.13, 4.4, 5.3, 5.5, 7.5 and 7.6

and 8.8  
 
         Total–      12                        (Chapter-III)  
 
(iv)    Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are   still 
awaited: 7.7, 2.8, 4.8, 8.9 and 8.10 
 
 
                                           Total-        5                       (Chapter-IV) 
 
 
 
 
 
 

1 
 
CHAPTER I  
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRRY 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.1 The Committee is of the firm view that the Ministry needs to make concerted efforts for 
liquidation of pending UCs. Taking into account mounting number of pending UCs and the 
thousand of crores of fund blocked, the Committee s trongly recommends setting up of a 
monitoring cell to monitor the pendency of UCs and coordinate and liaise with the defaulting 
States/UTs aggressively. 
(Para 2.24) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 NMPB/NAM has set up a monitoring cell within the Accounts  
Division to monitor the pendency of UCs and coordinate and liaise with the defaulting States/UTs 
aggressively. 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.3 The Committee takes note of the increasing volume of export of medicinal plants but is not 
satisfied with the pace of its growth. The Comm ittee feels that India is rich in unique and 
expensive medicinal plants having vast potential export of such plants, but appropriate focus and 
priority needs to be given. 
(Para 3.9) 
Action Taken  
 
1.4 In order to encourage Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs ) and Good Field Collection 
Practices (GFCPs) in medicinal plants and enhance quality and safety of their produce, the 
Government has launched the Voluntary Certification Scheme for Medicinal Plants Produce 
(VCSMPP) on 22nd November, 2017. 
  
1.5 Regional Workshops are being organised among stakeholders to create greater awareness 
about VCSMPP Schemes. 
  
1.6 For global promotion and support to Indian Medicinal Plants sector, the Ministry of 
AYUSH, Government of India has developed a standard “Memorandum of U nderstanding 
(MOU) for bilateral cooperation in the field of medicinal plants”.   So far, the bilateral MoUs for 
cooperation in the field of medicinal plants have been signed with Trinidad & Tobago, Sao Tome 
& Principe, Equatorial Guinea and Bangladesh. 
  
1.7 Government has provided higher incentive for herbs falling under ITC HS subheading 
121190 under Merchandise Exports from India (MEIS) scheme for boosting country’s exports of 
herbs.  Under the said scheme incentive @ 3%, 5% and 7% is provided. 
 
 
 
 

2 
 
III. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8 The Committee would also like to emphasize that India is known to be a treasure trove of 
medicinal plants. What is required is to identify, conserve and gratefully use them for medicinal 
purposes. Theref ore, focus of the Board should be on utilizing the rich biodiversity on a 
sustainable basis. The Committee would also like to highlight the pivotal role that the local 
community can play in development, conservation and sustainable use of such plants. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends the NMPB to popularize a programme for sustainable 
development of Medicinal Plants amongst the local community. 
(Para 3.13) 
Action Taken 
 
1.9 For Sustainable Development of medicinal Plants amongst the local communitie s (Joint 
Forest Management Committees (JFMCs)/Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs), 
Panchayats/Van Panchayats etc.), there is a provision under “Central Sector Scheme on 
Conservation, Development and Sustainable Management of Medicinal Plants” of NMPB .  As 
per the said scheme guidelines financial assistance of Rs.15.00 Lakh per JFMCs/BMCs etc. is 
provided for creation of primary processing facilities in the form of Drying   Yards, Storage 
Godowns etc. for value addition of medicinal plants raw material and thereby generating 
livelihood to the local communities. 
  
1.10 Under “Central Sector Scheme on Conservation, Development and Sustainable 
Development of Medicinal Plants”, National Medicinal Plant Board supports for Medicinal Plants 
Conservation Areas (MPCDAs) and resource augmentation as project mode.   MPCDAs cover on 
an average area of 200 hectares or smaller areas in case of endemic and critically endangered 
species.  As per guideline, financial assistance of @20,000 per hectare is provided. 
  
1.11 In addition, resource augmentation of medicinal plant species assisted through natural 
regeneration and artificial regeneration of local populations of medicinal and aromatic plant.   
Active interest and engagement of rural communities in such a conservation program is 
instrumental to address sustainability of the medicinal plant sector as a whole, hence financial 
support also provided for community mobilization through entry point activities etc. 
  
1.12 Under “Central Sector Scheme on Conservation, Developmen t and Sustainable 
development of Medicinal Plants”, under which there is a provision to provide project based 
support to various Government and Non -Government organizations to establish various types of 
herbal garden to popularize the usefulness of commonl y available and frequently used Medicinal 
Plants among the various stakeholders and sensitize the public about our traditional knowledge. It 
is also a way of conserving Rare, Endangered and Threatened (RET) species of Medicinal 
Plants.  Setting up of Herba l Gardens are promoted under the scheme to create awareness about 
traditional usage of medicinal plants. 
 

3 
 
IV.  QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDA, SIDDHA, UNANI AND 
HOMOEOPATHIC (AYUSH) DRUGS 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.13 The Committee time and again has been emphasizin g upon a stringent regulatory 
framework for quality control of ASU&H drugs. The Committee believes that for AYUSH 
systems to emerge as a strong alternative system of medicine, it is imperative that its credibility is 
enhanced through proper monitoring, qua lity control of drugs by scientific validation, proper 
parameters for clinical trials, upgradation of drug testing labs, GMP compliance by manufacturing 
units, control of misleading advertisements, etc. The Committee taking note of all the 
achievements would like to recommend that quality control of ASU&H drugs is one of the most 
important areas within the AYUSH ambit which needs to be accorded utmost priority. There is 
also a need for integration of AYUSH system of medicine with the modern system which is only 
possible through scientific validation and strict quality control for safety and efficacy of this 
system of medicine. The Committee strongly recommends for expediting and bringing forth the 
legislation for a regulatory umbrella for the education and p rofession of Pharmacy in Indian 
Medicine and Homoeopathy.   
(Para 4.4) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14 The Ministry has taken note of the recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee and 
would like to inform that Pharmacopoeia Commission of Indian Medicine and Homeopathy, 
Pharmacopoeia Laboratory of Indian Medicine and Homeopathic Pharmacopoeia Laboratory 
have been set up. These organisations are mandated to develop the quality standards of Ayurveda, 
Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy (ASU&H) Drugs and publish the Pharmacopoeia.  
Pharmacopoeia are the regulatory document for the purpose of quality control of ASU&H drugs.  
  
1.15 The Cabinet in its meeting held on 03.06.2020 has approved the establishment of 
PCIM&H as subordinate office under Ministry of AYUSH by merging PLIM & HPL  both 
subordinate offices and PCIM&H an autonomous organization under Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
1.16 Similarly, the setting up of the regulatory framework through Pharmacy Council of Indian 
Medicine and Homoeopathy Bill, 2020 is being steered for approval of the  Cabinet and thereafter 
introduction of the same in the Parliament.   
 
 
V. PHARMA COVIGILENCE INITIATIVES FOR ASU DRUGS 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.17 The Committee observes that a very low amount of allocation is being made for the scheme 
bearing a very vital mand ate. Even though the utilization of this paltry allocation is not quite 
satisfactory, the Committee is of the view that adequate and an enhanced allocation for this scheme 
is essential to create a strong Pharmacovigilance network across the country so as t o ensure 
effective control of misleading advertisements, safety monitoring of ASU&H drugs, 
documentations and analysis of Adverse Drug Reactions, etc. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends sufficient enhancement of funds for the scheme at RE stage. 
(Para 5.3) 

4 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.18 The network of Pharmacovigilance centres of ASU&H drugs is getting established and 
more peripheral pharmacovigilance centres have been added to the network. Accordingly, the 
recommendations of the Hon'ble Parliamentary Committee has b een noted and   provision of Rs. 
2.83 crore has been made in the B.E. 2020 -21, which can be appropriately enhanced in 
accordance with the proposal of requirement of funds from Pharmacovigilance Centres.   
 
Recommendation 
 
1.19 The Committee noting the vario us initiatives being taken under the scheme of 
Pharmacovigilance initiatives, observes that the Ministry is in the process of building a 
network/structure for carrying out strict monitoring/vigilance of quality control of ASU&H drugs. 
The Committee feels that this 3-tier network of pharmacovigilance needs to play pro -active role in 
reporting adverse drug events along with surveillance of misleading advertisements. With the 
Steering & Monitoring Committee, Technical Advisory Committee and Central Signal Dete ction 
& Causality Assessment Committee have been set up to assist in efficient implementation action of 
the said scheme, the Committee hopes that the task relating to the well -being of patients 
consuming ASU&H drugs will be taken care of. The Committee emp hasizes upon the need for 
imparting training and capacity building and also the awareness generation of ASU&H 
Pharmacovigilance so as to educate all involved in the network of pharmacovigilance for 
successful implementation of the scheme. 
(Para 5.5) 
Action Taken 
 
1.20 In order to successfully implement the scheme and for imparting training and generating 
awareness, three (3) CME training programs were conducted by the Intermediary 
Pharmacovigilance Centres of Ayurveda and Unani. Forty (40) public awareness programs have 
been conducted by the Peripheral Pharmacovigilance Centres to develop better understanding

II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.1 The Committee is disappointed to note that against the projected demand of Rs. 5035.27 
crore for 2020-21, the Ministry of AYUSH has been allocated Rs. 2122.08 crores reflecting huge 
shortfall of Rs. 2913.19 crores. The budgetary estimates of 2020 -21 when compared with RE 
2019-20 indicate a marginal increase of Rs. 265.08 crores only for the Ministry. The Committ ee 
appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry to get enhanced allocation but could not succeed. The 
Committee is constrained to note that several schemes of the Ministry would be affected due to 
shortfall of funds. The Committee apprehends that the objec tives of important schemes like 
National Ayush Mission, Health and Wellness centres etc would not be fulfilled due to financial 
constraints. Moreover, several research projects, construction work of National Institutes and 
Research Councils would also get affected. The Committee takes note of submission of the 
Ministry to make up the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of Rs.1000 crore from Higher 
Education Funding Agency (HEFA), to support, in particular, the 8 construction projects of 
National Institutes. The Committee is surprised to note that financial constraints have forced the 
Ministry to raise loan which shows that Government is not very serious towards promoting 
AYUSH and letting it emerge as an alternative and economical system of medicine. The 
Committee, however, is of the view that that the Ministry, being a relatively new one requires 
adequate funds and resources for proving its efficacy and worth. The Committee, in its previous 
Reports, has consistently been emphasizing upon substantial increas e in the allocation to the 
Ministry for executing its various schemes/programmes. The Committee, therefore, strongly, 
recommends the Ministry to approach Ministry of Finance at RE stage with the request for 
additional demand so that implementations of sche mes of the Ministry are not affected, adversely. 
It also recommends to the Ministry to utilize the allocated funds optimally with focus on the 
priority areas and make best use of the available funds. 
(Para 2.4) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.2 It is a fact that this Min istry has been allocated an amount of Rs. 2,122.08 crore for the 
year 2020-21 as against the projected demand of Rs. 5,025.37 crore, which is only 3.26 per cent 
of the Health Budget.   Apart from the above, this Ministry has already moved a proposal to 
obtain a loan of Rs.1,000.00 crore from Higher Education Finance Agency (HEFA) to augment 
fund for the work projects being undertaken by the various National Institutes functioning under 
this Ministry.   The proposal is under the active consideration at the app ropriate level in the 
Ministry of Finance.  Since the allocation was less than the projected requirements, this Ministry 
had taken up the matter immediately on receipt of the allocation with senior level officers of the 
Ministry of Finance including the Fi nance Minister to apprise them of the inadequacy of Budget 
allocation vis-à-vis the projection.  Further, as recommended by the Committee, this Ministry will 
also take up the issue again at the RE stage for increasing the allocation.  Further, the endeavour  
and efforts of this Ministry is to utilize the funds allotted optimally, but in some cases the 

10 
 
utilization could not be achieved due to non -approval/late approval of some schemes during the 
year despite best efforts put in by the Ministry. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.3 The Committee is of the considered view that lower budgetary allocation (Rs.2,122.08 
crores) against the projected demand of (Rs.5025.21 crore) in BE 2020 -21 would not make the 
Ministry capable of achieving its mandate to develop AYUSH System  as the preferred system of 
living and practice for attaining a healthy India.  The Committee had in its 108th Report 
recommended that at least 5% of the total health b udget should be allocated to the Ministry of 
AYUSH. However, the actual allocation remai ned at 3.26%, as a result of which the physical 
performance of various construction projects and schemes viz. National AYUSH Mission Health 
and Wellness centre viz -a-viz originally conceived plan would definitely suffer.  The Ministry is 
now compelled to m eet the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of Rs. 1000 crores from Higher 
Education Funding Agency to support the 8 construction projects of National Institutes and on -
going schemes.  
 
3.4 The Committee, however, would  also like to be apprised of the sta tus of loan of Rs.1000 
crore from Higher Education Finance Agency (HEFA) and the response of the Ministry of 
Finance to the request of Ministry of AYUSH for higher allocation at RE Stage keeping in view 
the inadequacy of budgetary allocation viz -a-viz  pro jected demand at RE Stage.   The 
Committee would also like to be informed of the final appropriation of allocated budget, viz -a-
viz projected allocation at RE Stage on various Schemes of the Ministry and the status note on 
the physical achievement of vario us schemes due to lower budgetary allocation.  Such s tatus 
note should also reflect the actual physical achievement against the objective set under various 
schemes at the time of projecting demand at BE Stage.   Given the imminent need for higher 
allocation of funds to the Ministry, the Committee reiterates its recommendation of allocating at 
least 5% of the total Health Budget for the Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.5  The Committee notes a difference of Rs. 1693.3 crore in the projected demand of Rs.  
4469.59 crore in BE 2019-20 and the demand of Rs. 2776.29 crore at the RE stage. This, according 
to the Committee, speaks volumes not only about the paradigms shift in its original conceived 
schemes but also utilization capacity of the Ministry. The Commi ttee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry must make realistic assessment of its fund requirement keeping in view on -going 
projects/projects to be undertaken and accordingly project its demand. 
(Para 2.5) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.6 With regard to less projectio n of funds at RE Stage as compared to the BE stage, it may 
be mentioned that the projection made in Budget Estimates are generally made keeping in view 
the prospective plan and execution of the projects during the course of the entire financial year, 
whereas while projecting the requirement at RE stage it is purely based on the actual balance 
work/requirement to be carried out during the remaining period of the Financial Year keeping in 
mind the scope of   utilization of fund allotted in RE which  are generally made available to the 
Programme Divisions  in the fag end of the Financial Year after due process of formalities such 

11 
 
as obtaining of supplementary grant and issue of re -appropriation orders etc.. Therefore, the 
projection of the requirement at RE stage  is made which is more realistic vis -à-vis availability of 
fund and time. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.7 The Committee is not convinced with Ministry's response  that projection  made at BE 
stage is generally made keeping in view the prospective plan and the progress made in 
execution of projects during the entire financial year. The Committee believes that the 
ambitious and lofty plans of the Ministry must be commensurate to its capacity to utilize the 
funds optimally and therefore, the projection should not be far -fetched and unrealistic .  In 
fact, realistic assessment of what can actually be achieved and spent in one financial year 
should be done.  The Committee,  therefore, is of the view that the Ministry should be more 
cautious and grounded in its financial projections. 
 
3.8 The Committee, at the same time, is constrained to observe that the Ministry of AYUSH 
falls short of the target of optimum utilization of allocated funds due to non -approval /late 
approval of some Schemes.  This argument speaks poorly about the state of affairs in terms of 
the decision making process and monitoring capacity of the Ministry. The Committee, in this 
regard, observes that all the formalities/procedures viz., obtaining supplementary demands and 
issuance of re -appropriation or der must be completed without waiting for the fag -end of the 
financial year. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for timely approval of schemes 
as well as timely release of fund for ensuring completion of projects within scheduled time and 
without cost over-run.

administrative which could have easily been avoided had there been proper prudential monitoring
